adjudication.reason: The gold has 'Sē se þē lufað, sē þē sǣcð; sē se þē fylið, sē þē hæfð', with all four þē long. This translates Soliloquia I.1.3 'quem attendere...amare; quem videre...habere' ('he who follows thee has thee'), so the target is acc. 'thee'. Hargrove separates the particle from the pronoun elsewhere (00041 'þe þē flȳgð'), so the system's short þe is the relative-particle reading, a class B function difference.

'hāwien ðes þe hēo gesēon wolden' has ðes = gen. ðæs 'that which' (Clark Hall: 'ðes = ðæs'). The long ðēs in the encoder's lexicon (Bright, WS Matthew, Wiktionary þēs) is only ever nom. masc. 'this'. The readings differ in lemma and case, so the class C label for þes 'this' does not apply to this token.

'ic wæs ǣac þes geðafa' is gen. þæs with geþafa 'consenting to that'. Hargrove also writes þes for gen. þæs in 00315 and 00490. The system's þēs exists in the lexicon only as nom. 'this' (Bright, Matthew, Wiktionary), so the readings differ in case and lemma.

'tō ðe cymð' can only be the pronoun 'thee', and Hargrove writes tō þē/ðē long 21 of 22 times, so the short gold is a slip. Under the prose rule (type by steps 4 to 6), gold and system are the same pronoun in the same function and only the marking differs. 'Grammatical' would wrongly imply the gold reads the relative particle.

'mǣstne anweald' means 'greatest power' in both readings. BT cites the same verse (Mt 28:18 'ǣlc ánweald') under án-weald that Bright's WS Matthew prints as anweald. The BT supplement also says many an-weald passages may belong under either form, and Wiktionary gives 'power' under ānweald. So the dictionaries disagree on the length of one content word.

'befeste þe hālne Gode' is the reflexive pronoun 'thee', agreeing with acc. hālne, and Hargrove writes 'befeste ðē' long elsewhere. The short gold is a slip, and under the prose rule the two readings are the same pronoun with different marking.

In 'þinne cniht', þinne is the possessive 'thy'. Short þinne is listed in Wiktionary (etym. 2) and WikiPron /ˈθin.ne/ as a form of þynne 'thin'. No edition marks the possessive short by habit: WS Matthew has it once against 14 þīnne. That single Matthew slip in the training lexicon is why editorial stays defensible.

Tauber has con as pr3s of cunnan 'can' (l. 1746), and H&S, Wyatt, Clark Hall and Bright all have short con. The lexicon's long cōn comes only from Bright's misprint of cōm 'came' (Ælfric's Preface to Genesis, 'tō mannum cōn and began'). BT's cón is a separate adjective headword, 'bold' (v. céne). So no source marks 'can' long, and editorial does not apply.

'līnan þæs āwriten' is the past participle of āwrītan (short ablaut grade). Wiktionary lists āwrīten as the present subjunctive plural, so the readings differ in inflection. No edition marks the participle long: āwriten appears in Bright, Sweet, Zupitza, Matthew and Hargrove, and āwrīten in none of them.

Tauber has wesan as the infinitive 'be' (l. 3021), and H&S and Wyatt both have wesan. The system's wēsan is a separate verb, 'to soak, macerate' (Clark Hall ±wēsan, BT wésan 'to steep, soak', Wiktionary wesan etym. 3). Two content words under different headwords make this a homograph.

Tauber has minne as asm of min 'my' (l. 2012), and H&S and Wyatt both have mīnne. In the CharsiuG2P lexicon, short minne is only Bright's Wanderer 'minne wisse', deliberately short next to two mīnne in the same sentence (Clark Hall: minne II = myne 'love'), and WikiPron /ˈmin.ne/ = min 'small, vile'. No training edition marks the possessive short, so the editorial habit condition fails. The class column is empty.

Same as 270: Tauber has mīnne asm 'my' (l. 638), and both editions have mīnne. Short minne in the lexicon is only myne 'love' (Bright, Clark Hall) or min 'small' (Wiktionary/WikiPron), never the possessive marked short.

This is the conjunction þæt in 'geearnian þǣt ic sī wurðe', and gold þǣt is a sporadic Hargrove marking (4 of about 653). The guidelines say a doubtful prose gold is typed by steps 4 to 6, not as 'other'. The two readings are the same word and function, and Sweet's Primer also has þǣt, which makes the skeleton class C.

The article þæt in 'forlǣt hē þǣt scyp' is the same word and function in both readings, and only the marking differs. Under the prose rule a sporadic gold þǣt is typed by steps 4 to 6, which gives editorial (class C þæt|þǣt). 'Other' is not the route the guidelines set for prose.

adjudication.reason: H&S slip in its own text at l.537: its glossary says 'geoguð-feorh ... on geogoð- (geoguð-) fēore, 537, 2665', so the editors meant the vowel long (dat. of feorh, compensatory lengthening). Wyatt fēore and Tauber/Brunetti ġeogoðfēore agree. H&S's other unmarked feore (934 tō wīdan feore, 1844 on swā geongum feore) are deliberate and the glossary confirms them, so they do not count against this.

Probable Wyatt slip at l.25. Wyatt prints geþēon at 910, has no footnote at 25, and marks other contracted forms long where meter needs uncontracted scansion (slēa 681, flēon 820, tēon 1036), so he has no convention of leaving such forms unmarked. Tauber/Brunetti also leaves 25 unmarked, but that follows its own general metrical convention (it also has slea, fleon, teon), so the match is not evidence of a choice by Wyatt. H&S glossary: ge-þēon, 25, 911.

H&S slip, not our processing: the raw Gutenberg text has 'Mod Þrȳðo wæg' (l.1931). H&S reads mōd 'pride' as the object of wæg (its note credits the name 'Modthrytho' to G. and does not adopt it), and it marks mōd and every mōd- compound long elsewhere (mōd 7x, glossary mōd st. n.). Wyatt has Mōd.

H&S prints the damaged l.2221 diplomatically ('þæt sie . . . . ðioð . . . . . / . idh . folc-beorn') and leaves it unglossed: sīe under wesan cites only 435 and 683, and nothing cites 2221 under se/sēo. So 'sie' is a bare MS fragment, not a vowel-length decision. Wyatt reads sīe (Tauber nsf seo, sīe). Calling it a deliberate editorial choice is arguable, but the guideline's 'really mark its vowel length differently' is not met.

Wyatt omission at l.144. Every source has a long vowel: rīxian/rīcsian in B-T, Clark Hall and Wiktionary, H&S glossary 'pret. sg. rīxode, 144', Tauber rīxode, and Bright and the WS Matthew rīxode/rīxað. Wyatt marks rīcsian at 2211, and long vowels before x elsewhere (līxte 3x, wrīxlan), so it is not a policy of shortening before x.

The editions read different words at l.1783. H&S's note on l.1784 cites the conjecture wigge geweorðad 'honored in war', and its glossary has 'wīg-ge-weorðad, pret. part., war-honored, 1784?', so the macron marks the wīg- element (Tauber also has wīggeweorþad), while plain dat. wigge stays unmarked at 1657/1771. Wyatt's footnote on 1783 says 'I have followed the MS.' and reads dat. wigge + weorþad, unmarked like his other wigge.
